inline.s: [At one stroke raise your spirit and leap up to the summit, to the peak of the sheer cliff, the top of the precipice. Let the body plunge straight down, let go the hand and range at will; wipe out the traces and sweep away the tracks, leaving not a thread. If the seventh consciousness does not die, how can the Dharma-body live?]

At one stroke raise your spirit and leap up to the summit, to the peak of the sheer cliff, the top of the precipice. Then let the body plunge straight down (no longer minutely examining and investigating who it is that is aware, but gathering the mind into quiet illumination), let go the hand and range at will; wipe out the traces and sweep away the tracks, leaving not a thread. If the seventh consciousness (manas) does not die, how can the Dharma-body live?

[At one stroke raise your spirit and leap up to the summit, to the peak of the sheer cliff, the top of the precipice] At one stroke carry the practice of “minutely examining and investigating who it is that is aware” to its utmost, like a cold fire drawing smoke, a single thread stretching on unbroken. [Let the body plunge straight down, let go the hand and range at will] No longer minutely examining and investigating, one enters quiet illumination — that is, the “gathering of the mind into quiet illumination” spoken of below. On this, the Elder Master Xuyun instructs:

“At this time it is clear and pure, empty and hollow. If the feeling of doubt is gone, then it is the indeterminate state, sitting upon the withered-wood rock, or what is called ‘soaking a stone in cold water.’ At this point one must raise it — to raise is to be aware and illumine. Awareness, which is not to be deluded, is wisdom; illumination, which is not to be scattered, is concentration. This single thought, settled and quietly illumined, unmoved in its suchness, knowing and not dark, clear and ever aware, is like a cold fire drawing smoke, a single thread stretching on unbroken. When one's practice reaches this point, one must have the diamond eye, and no longer raise it; to raise it then is to put a head on top of a head.”
(The Elder Master Xuyun's Expedient Instructions

Instructions in the Chan Hall) [When one's practice reaches this point] “This single thought, settled and quietly illumined, unmoved in its suchness, knowing and not dark, clear and ever aware, like a cold fire drawing smoke, a single thread stretching on unbroken.” [No longer raise] At this time, though one no longer raises awareness-illumination, its illumination is still there, illumining of itself — this is called quiet illumination. In stillness it is ever illumining, in illumination it is ever still. Master Dayu's gatha says: “In quiet illumination, illumining the still — above all avoid using force. To become a Buddha and be master — there is no other secret.” This is speaking of the state of quiet illumination. [If the seventh consciousness does not die, how can the Dharma-body live?] This is what this book (The Ontology of the Universe of Myriad Things) said earlier: “When the seventh consciousness is greatly dead, the Dharma-body at once lives.” [When the seventh consciousness is greatly dead, the Dharma-body at once lives] The seventh consciousness (manas), falsely clinging to body and mind as self, unceasingly seizes upon the dharma-dust within the alaya-consciousness to supply the sixth consciousness (the intellect) with its thinking. Therefore when the seventh consciousness (manas) is greatly dead (no longer holding to attachments and delusions), the Dharma-body at once lives.

[In walking, standing, sitting, and lying, never leave the practice. The mind like wood or stone, as if dull and as if benumbed; if it is not thus, one cannot reach the ultimate. Gathering the mind into quiet illumination, fine and close, intimate and keen. Pressed to the utmost, mountains end and waters run out. When the occasion ripens, and one knocks against it and touches it, sees a form or hears a sound, of a sudden one is startled and wakes. Peas popping in cold ash — after the ultimate, revival. The clouds part and the sky is clear; body and mind are of a sudden still, the body the same as empty space, sweat drenching the whole frame, and one is suddenly and completely awakened. The light of self-nature's wisdom is wholly revealed, the still-wisdom arises, and the ten directions are vast and clear. The luminous
hào
sun hangs in the sky, roundly illumining everything.]

In walking, standing, sitting, and lying, one must never leave the practice of quiet illumination. The mind like wood or stone, as if dull and as if benumbed; if it is not thus, one cannot reach the ultimate. Gathering the mind into quiet illumination, fine and close, intimate and keen, until it is pressed to the utmost, when mountains end and waters run out. When the occasion ripens, and one knocks against it and touches it, sees a form or hears a sound, of a sudden one is startled and wakes (awakened). Then peas pop in cold ash — after the ultimate, revival. At this time the clouds part and the sky is clear, body and mind are of a sudden still, the body the same as empty space, sweat drenching the whole frame, and one is suddenly and wholly awakened. The light of self-nature's wisdom is wholly revealed, the still-wisdom arises, and the ten directions are vast and clear. The light of self-nature's wisdom is like the luminous sun hanging in the sky, roundly illumining everything.

[After the ultimate, revival] To have swooned into a death (that is, what this passage calls “the mind like wood or stone, as if dull and as if benumbed”) and then to come back to life (that is, what this passage calls “suddenly and wholly awakened, the light of self-nature's wisdom wholly revealed,

the luminous sun hanging in the sky, roundly illumining everything”). “After the ultimate, revival” is the great dying and great living so often spoken of in the Chan school: one must be greatly dead for a time before one can be greatly alive. The Blue Cliff Record says:
“One must be greatly dead for a time, and only then, when revived, does one attain it.”
This is also
“letting go the entire body, only then is there a share of freedom.”
[Vast and clear (kuò rán)] The state of empty stillness.

[Passing through the three passes, of a sudden one attains no-birth; wisdom pervades the dharma-realm, and the Way realizes true permanence. One directly realizes the store-nature and directly sees the original. This is what is called the great sea of extinction, the great nature of self-mastery, the great light of wisdom, the great method of liberation. With birth and death extinguished, quiescent extinction is joy. The dust-afflictions of the guest are from now on forever extinguished. Warm or cold, one knows it for oneself, and does not reveal it to others. Just with this place of awakening, one passes through situations to test the mind, follows conditions to sustain and maintain it, cherishes and nourishes it as an infant, and purifies away the flowing consciousness, smelting it into true wisdom.]

Thereupon passing through the three passes (illuminating the mind and seeing the nature, cutting off all afflictions, and realizing the patience of no-birth), of a sudden one coalesces with the principle of no-birth (realizing the patience of no-birth); wisdom pervades the dharma-realm, and the Way realizes true permanence. One directly realizes the Tathagata-store and directly sees the original. This is what is called the great sea of extinction, the great nature of self-mastery, the great light of wisdom, the great method of liberation. With birth and death extinguished, quiescent extinction is joy. The dust-afflictions of the guest are from now on forever extinguished. The scenery here — like a person drinking water, one knows for himself whether it is warm or cold — is not revealed to others. Just with this place of awakening, one passes through situations to test the mind, follows conditions to sustain and maintain it, cherishes and nourishes the holy embryo, and purifies away the present manifest karmic flowing consciousness, smelting it into true wisdom.

[Three passes] First, break the first pass, to illuminate the mind and see the nature; second, break the heavy pass, to cut off all afflictions; third, break the prison pass, to realize the patience of no-birth. [Tathagata-store] That is, the original nature. (For detail, see
Mind, Self-Nature, and the Tathagata-Store
) [True wisdom] The wisdom that clearly understands the true mark of reality, also called “holy wisdom.”
[No-birth] Nirvana has no arising and no ceasing, so it is called “no-birth.” The Perfect Awakening Sutra says:
“All sentient beings, within no-birth, falsely see arising and ceasing; therefore they are spoken of as turning the wheel of birth and death.”
The Sutra of the Most Excellent Sovereign says:
“No-birth is real; birth is false and vain. The foolish, drowning in birth and death; the Tathagata embodies the real, with no falsehood, and this is called nirvana.”

[Patience of no-birth] Also called the patience of the no-birth of dharmas: true wisdom abides in the principle that “all dharmas originally never arose and therefore never cease,” never again falling back. The patience of the no-birth of dharmas is the bodhisattva's realization of the ultimate emptiness of all dharmas. The Great Prajna Sutra says:

“Thus the irreversible bodhisattva-mahasattva, by means of the emptiness of self-mark, contemplates all dharmas, having entered the bodhisattva's upright nature apart from birth, even to the point of seeing not a single dharma as obtainable. Because it is unobtainable, there is no contrivance. Because there is no contrivance, there is ultimately no birth. Because of ultimate no-birth, it is called the patience of the no-birth of dharmas. Because one attains such patience of the no-birth of dharmas, one is called the irreversible bodhisattva-mahasattva.”
